title: Problem Overview
content: **Erdős Problem #605** asks whether repeated distances on a sphere can grow superlinearly. Given n points on a 2-sphere, how many pairs can share the same distance? If u_D(n) is the maximum such count for a sphere of radius D, does u_D(n)/n → ∞? The answer is YES, established by Erdős-Hickerson-Pach (1989) and strengthened by Swanepoel-Valtr (2004).
mathContext: The function u_D(n) is the spherical analogue of the classical unit distance function. The problem connects discrete geometry, incidence geometry, and algebraic constructions on surfaces.

title: Sphere and Point Configurations
content: We define a **sphere** of radius r as the set of points in ℝ³ at distance r from the origin. A **SphereConfig** is a set of n distinct points, all lying on the sphere. The structure enforces both membership (all points on the sphere) and injectivity (all points distinct).
mathContext: Working in EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) gives us access to Mathlib's inner product space and metric space machinery. The norm ‖p‖ = r condition defines the sphere.

title: Counting Distance Pairs
content: For a configuration, we count **ordered pairs** (i, j) with i < j at distance exactly d. The function countPairsAtDist returns this count, while maxRepeatedDist finds the maximum over all distances. We want maxRepeatedDist to grow superlinearly in n.
mathContext: The restriction i < j avoids double-counting. The maximum is taken over all distances that actually appear in the configuration, computed as a supremum over pairs.

title: The Function u_D(n)
content: **u_D(n)** is the central quantity: the maximum number of repeated-distance pairs achievable by any configuration of n points on a sphere of radius D. Defined as sSup (supremum) over all configurations. The question is whether u_D(n) grows faster than linearly in n.
mathContext: Formally, u_D(n) = sup{maxRepeatedDist(config) | config is a SphereConfig(n, D)}. This is an extremal function in the style of Turán-type problems.

title: Superlinear Growth Definition
content: **superlinearGrowth(D)** formalizes Erdős's question: for every constant C, there exists N such that u_D(n) ≥ C·n for all n ≥ N. This is equivalent to u_D(n)/n → ∞, meaning the repeated-distance count grows strictly faster than any linear function.
mathContext: This is the standard ε-N definition of a function tending to infinity, applied to the ratio u_D(n)/n. It captures 'superlinear' without specifying the exact growth rate.

title: Iterated Logarithm
content: **log*(n)** counts how many times you must apply the logarithm before reaching ≤ 1. It grows unimaginably slowly: log*(2) = 1, log*(16) = 3, log*(65536) = 4, and log*(2^65536) = 5. Despite this glacial growth, it does tend to infinity — which is all Erdős needed.
mathContext: Defined recursively: iterLog(n) = 0 for n ≤ 1, and 1 + iterLog(⌊log n⌋) otherwise. The EHP 1989 bound uses this function, making it historically significant even though Swanepoel-Valtr later improved it.

title: Erdős-Hickerson-Pach Bound (1989)
content: The **first superlinear bound**: u_D(n) ≥ c·n·log*(n) for spheres of radius D > 1. This landmark result resolved Problem #605 affirmatively. The proof uses a recursive geometric construction related to the Borsuk-Ulam theorem.
mathContext: Axiomatized because the proof requires sophisticated geometric arguments involving spherical configurations and topological methods not available in Mathlib.

title: Swanepoel-Valtr Bound (2004)
content: The **best known lower bound**: u_D(n) ≥ c·n·√(log n) for D > 1. This vastly improves EHP — for n = 10^100, √(log n) ≈ 15 while log*(n) ≈ 5. The proof uses algebraic geometry on the sphere to construct point sets with many repeated distances.
mathContext: The improvement from log*(n) to √(log n) is enormous in practice, even though both are subpolynomial. The √(log n) factor is the current frontier of knowledge for general spheres.

title: Upper Bound: n^{4/3}
content: For **all** radii D > 0, u_D(n) ≤ C·n^{4/3}. This universal upper bound comes from incidence geometry — specifically, the Szemerédi-Trotter theorem adapted to points and circles in three dimensions.
mathContext: The exponent 4/3 matches the √2 sphere lower bound, showing it cannot be improved in general. For other radii, the true growth may be much lower than n^{4/3}.

title: √2 Sphere: Tight Bound n^{4/3}
content: The sphere of radius **√2 is magical**: u(n) ≍ n^{4/3}, achieving the upper bound exactly. This happens because √2 is the circumradius of a unit cube — the 8 vertices of a cube inscribed in this sphere create 12 edges of equal length, and generalizations of this construction yield the n^{4/3} lower bound.
mathContext: The tight bound means both c·n^{4/3} ≤ u(n) ≤ C·n^{4/3} for constants c, C > 0. This is the only known radius achieving n^{4/3}.

title: Main Theorem: Erdős #605 Solved
content: **The answer is YES.** For any sphere of radius D > 1, repeated distances grow superlinearly: u_D(n)/n → ∞. The proof combines the Swanepoel-Valtr bound u_D(n) ≥ c·n·√(log n) with the fact that √(log n) → ∞.
mathContext: The theorem erdos_605 states superlinearGrowth(D) for all D > 1. It follows from erdos_605_superlinear, which is axiomatized since the full proof chain requires analysis beyond basic Lean tactics.

title: Witness Function
content: An explicit witness for Problem #605: **f(n) = √(log n)** satisfies f(n) → ∞ and u_D(n) ≥ f(n)·n for large n. This is the strongest known witness function for general spheres.
mathContext: Stated using Filter.Tendsto for the divergence condition, matching Mathlib's formalism for limits at infinity.

title: Unit Distance Connection
content: The classical **planar unit distance problem** asks how many pairs at distance 1 can occur among n points in ℝ². Problem #605 extends this to spherical surfaces. The sphere allows more repeated distances than the plane for large radii.
mathContext: The planar bound is Θ(n^{1+c/log log n}), barely superlinear. The spherical bound n·√(log n) is of a different character, reflecting the richer geometric structure of curved surfaces.

title: Geometric Constructions
content: **Great circles** give linear bounds: n points equally spaced on a great circle yield Ω(n) repeated-distance pairs. **Cube vertices** on the √2 sphere give 12 pairs among 8 points. The superlinear bounds require more sophisticated algebraic constructions.
mathContext: The cube_vertices_bound axiom states u(√2, 8) ≥ 12, corresponding to the 12 edges of a cube. Each edge of a unit cube inscribed in a √2 sphere has length 2.
